newsitem.title: UK: British ruling party split again on Europe.
newsitem.headline: British ruling party split again on Europe.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives have been plunged into bitter conflict once again over the European Union, with finance minister Kenneth Clarke under fire from right-wingers angry at his support of a single EU currency.

Clarke enraged members of his own party opposed to closer links with the EU by warning in a weekend interview that Britain could lose its opportunity of joining a single currency if it "dithered" about entering at the start.
Bill Cash, a leading member of parliament on the so-called Eurosceptic wing of the party, said on Monday that Prime Minister John Major should "consider his (Clarke's) position".

Cash, who said he was backed by a "significant" number of people in the party, maintained that moves towards a single currency were hurting Britain and causing unemployment in Europe. Eurosceptics want Major categorically to rule out joining a single currency.

"The government, in particular Kenneth Clarke, are actually allowing the bending of the rules in order to allow the whole process (of monetary union) to go along when instead of surfing with it we should be trying to beach it," Cash said.

Major has sought to bridge the divide between Eurosceptics and pro-Europeans like Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke by saying Britain will make its mind up about a single currency, due to start in 1999, when all ramifications of monetary union have been addressed.

Cash's remarks come on top of a stream of criticism of Clarke, including a suggestion by former party chairman Norman Tebbit that Major should rule out British entry into a single currency even if that meant Clarke quit the cabinet.
"If it resulted in victory at the general election, clearly it would be a price worth paying," Tebbit said.
The weekend comments by Tebbit, a key member of former prime minister Margaret Thatcher's team, angered Clarke, who was speaking at a meeting of European finance ministers in Dublin.

"I wish that Norman Tebbit would devote his considerable rhetorical and political talents to trying to get the government elected and not continually trying to open up political division about central policy," said Clarke.

Clarke, who predicted in Dublin that a single currency would come into force "around the turn of the century" with between six and eight EU member states participating, said a British decision to stay outside would be a major mistake.
"That would be the worst policy of all, of the British doing their traditional business of not be able to make their minds up and then joining late. That would be pathetic," he said.
"If they went ahead without us, they would do great harm to the whole union if it then began to break up."
John Redwood, who quit the cabinet last year to mount a failed bid to replace Major, said: "I think it is a great pity that the Chancellor has damaged the unity of the government.

"The government has not decided to rule out any option, indeed the government's one policy on this is they want to keep open all options... Clarke is trying to bounce the cabinet or he has forgotten what the collective line of the cabinet is."

Other pro-Europeans have begun fighting back against what they see as a rising tide of anti-EU feeling in the party, which faces an election in the next eight months and is about 20 points behind the opposition Labour Party in opinion polls.
Senior party figures, including former foreign secretary Douglas Hurd, last week warned that it would be a betrayal of Britain's national interest if Major ruled out joining the EU single currency.
